extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers, instrument-makers, and astronomers (members/readers of the Royal Society)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and results for conducting, describing, and interpreting experimental and observational work in natural philosophy (instrument design, astronomical observations, fluid/air experiments, and mathematical quadratures). Emphasis on instrument geometry, precise timing/measurement, experimental control, and appropriate mathematical methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lens/eye placement determines image orientation
rubrics_metrics.description: A single convex-glass cannot properly be said by itself to show objects erect or reverse, but in respect of placing of the eye that looks through it: if the eye be placed nearer to it than the focus, the objects are erect; if the eye be placed just in the focus, the objects are neither erect nor reversed (in confusion); and if the eye be placed further from the glass than the focus, the objects are reversed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use eye position relative to the lens focal point to predict observed orientation. The text gives explicit positional relations (eye nearer than focus → erect; at focus → confused; farther than focus → reversed) and notes that for distant objects rays may be treated as parallel toward the object-glass.

rubrics_metrics.name: Object-glass determines inversion in two-convex-lens telescopes
rubrics_metrics.description: In a telescope of two convex-glasses the reversion of objects proceeds wholly from the object-glass and its position; the eye-glass contributes nothing towards the rectification or reversion when the eye is placed in its focus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or designing a two-convex-lens telescope, attribute inversion to the object-glass and its placement; the eye-glass (with the eye at its focus) merely represents the species as formed in the distinct-base of the object-glass.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi-lens telescope can be considered as successive two-lens systems
rubrics_metrics.description: A telescope consisting of an object-glass and three eye-glasses is to be considered as two telescopes, each consisting of two convex-glasses: the first (object-glass + first eye-glass) inverts; the second (the two immediate eye-glasses) erects what the former inverted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For explanation/design, break multi-element convex systems into cascaded two-element systems to determine where inversion/erection occurs. The intermediate lenses primarily re-represent the image formed before them rather than actively inverting/erecting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique experimental comparisons that use deformable containers (bladder experiment)
rubrics_metrics.description: An experiment comparing the velocity of air and water by emptying a bladder (same weight and hole) is ingenious but flawed: the bladder filled with air yields and becomes flat when pressed, so the weight does not press every part equally as it does when the bladder remains distended (as with water); additionally water's own weight contributes to pressure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing fluids experimentally, control for container deformation and for differing effective pressures. Do not assume identical pressure application if one test subject (air) allows container collapse; design methods where the effective pressure on the fluids is truly comparable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hydrostatic method to deduce air velocity from jet heights and specific gravities
rubrics_metrics.description: From hydrostatic principles: of two different liquids urged by the same pressure, the one specifically lighter ascends higher, with heights reciprocally in the ratio of their specific gravities; velocities of bodies are as square roots of heights, so velocities of different fluids under same pressure are as roots of their specific gravities. Thus compute air velocity by finding equivalent water velocity under same pressure and multiplying by the square root ratio of specific gravities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Prop.1 and Prop.2: (1) heights ∝ 1/(specific gravity), (2) velocities ∝ sqrt(height) ⇒ velocities ∝ sqrt(1/(specific gravity)). Example given: using water head ~32 feet (velocity ≈45 ft/s) and approximate ratio water:air ≈840:1 gives air velocity ≈45×29 ≈1305 ft/s (with later correction noting mean atmospheric column ~33.5 ft giving ≈1348 ft/s). Use appropriate measured specific gravities and pressure equivalents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report precise timings and geometrical measures for occultations/eclipses
rubrics_metrics.description: Observational reports should give precise times for key phases (e.g., beginning/external contact, central immersion, internal contact/complete immersion, beginning of emersion, central/half emersion, complete emersion) and measure geometrical quantities (e.g., chord length across moon, planetary diameters measured by micrometer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide event times to the minute and second where possible (examples list times like 11:07:09 for beginning/external contact, 11:50:45 complete emersion). Include derived measurements (Jupiter diameter from micrometer and lunar-spot methods) and note observational conditions (e.g., time relative to full/new moon, libration) that affect interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and report local conditions when applying tide tables
rubrics_metrics.description: Tide behavior in a given port may differ from published general tables (e.g., the French ephemerides or Flamsteed's tide-tables). The same phase (quarter, new, full) can produce different timing relations in different ports or rivers; local winds (e.g., S.S.E. to S.S.W. blowing fresh) can prolong flow times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not apply tide tables from other ports without checking local observations; record local timings (examples: bar of Dublin high water times at new/full and quarter days) and note wind effects and port/rivers distances from the sea which modulate differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design criteria and observational procedure for a horizontal telescopic dial to observe time
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct a large horizontal dial adapted to local latitude, with divisions into minutes and parts, fitted with a large double gnomon and two pairs of moveable rulers (horizontal and gnomonic/stile rulers). Equip the stile ruler with telescopic sights and cross-hairs; use one pair of sights for morning/eastern stars and another for afternoon/western stars. Observing involves aiming through the stile ruler to center the sun/star and reading where the horizontal ruler cuts the dial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method avoids spherical triangle calculations and promises high precision (claims: accurate to within a quarter minute/15 seconds not lacking; can discern time to 3, 5, or 7 seconds using the telescopic sight). For star observations by night, use tables of temporary right ascensions and compute hour by adding horary distance to star's RA and subtracting sun's RA. Ensure dial is justly levelled and stated; design allows day or night use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of mathematical method for quadratures: infinite series vs Leibnitz's tangent method
rubrics_metrics.description: For inverting the problem of finding a curve from its tangent to determine quadratures, one may express areas of curves (e.g., circle, hyperbola) by infinite series when indefinite quadratures are 'impossible'; where series consist of irrational terms, use Leibnitz's method of finding tangents though the calculation may be more tedious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply series expansion methods to represent areas when possible and accept infinite-series expressions for curves like circle and hyperbola; revert to alternative tangent-based methods (Leibnitz) when series involve irrational terms that complicate direct expansion. Compare results with known expressions (e.g., Mercator, Newton) to validate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document observational context and compare like-for-like conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting observations (e.g., occultations), note contextual factors such as lunar phase, libration, time of day (day vs night observations affect stray light), observational method, and instrument limitations; compare measurements made under similar conditions (e.g., two occultations observed at different lunar phases yielding different apparent planetary diameters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state observational circumstances (e.g., 'it did not happen just at the full moon, but about a day after it' or 'measured in the day time adventitious rays were dispelled by sun's light'), and when possible justify preferring one measurement over another based on observational conditions.
